The attacker has two realistic supply-chain footholds: (i) they poison a small share of the fine-tuning data used to adapt the generator, and (ii) they write documents

text: a corpus and conditioning an LLM on them. The attacker has two realistic supply-chain footholds: (i) they poison a small share of the fine-tuning data used to adapt the generator, and (ii) they write documents into the knowledge base that the retriever indexes. I call this a dual-surface threat. The attacker is grey-box: they cannot read the retriever internals (embedding model, index) or the defender’s detection threshold. 1.2 Relevance and non-triviality Corpus injection alone is potent: as few as five malicious passages can exceed 90% attack success without touching the weights, and a fine-tuning backdoor makes the model emit attacker output on a hidden trigger while behaving normally otherwise. The dangerous case is the triggerless, stealthy document that is semantically normal in isolation, so it passes perdocument ingestion filters yet corrupts the answer only when co-retrieved with clean documents for

text: while behaving normally otherwise. The dangerous case is the triggerless, stealthy document that is semantically normal in isolation, so it passes perdocument ingestion filters yet corrupts the answer only when co-retrieved with clean documents for a specific query. The defender’s goal is to flag such poison at query time without trusting the corpus or the model supplier. The defence must not be trivially evadable: an attacker who knows it is deployed will adapt, so I explicitly test an adaptive attacker (Section 5). Research Question and Related Work 2.1 Prior attacks and defences Two attack surfaces are by now well established. Corpus poisoning injects malicious passages into the knowledge base: PoisonedRAG shows that a handful of crafted passages can control the answer, and TrojanRAG drives the behaviour through the retriever itself. Independently, weight-level backdoors implant a hidden trigger during training so

text: into the knowledge base: PoisonedRAG shows that a handful of crafted passages can control the answer, and TrojanRAG drives the behaviour through the retriever itself. Independently, weight-level backdoors implant a hidden trigger during training so the model misbehaves only on that trigger while passing normal evaluation. Defences against corpus poisoning cluster at two points in the pipeline. Ingestion-time filters score each document before indexing perplexity or rewriting filters, or embedding outlier detection, but by construction they judge documents in isolation and are weak against poison that is individually normal. Generation-time defences act after retrieval through robust aggregation over the answer, but need multiple generations or model internals. 2.2 The research gap Between these two defence points lies an unused surface: the retrieval layer at query time the assembled set of documents returned for a single query. No deployed defence inspects

No deployed defence inspects this set as a detection target, even though the most dangerous poison is anomalous precisely in context: a passage individually normal enough to survive ingestion filters, yet inconsistent with the genuine documents it is co-retrieved with. Prior work establishes corpus poisoning, weight-level backdoors, and ingestion/generation defences separately, but none targets the dual-surface threat with a query-time, retrieval-layer detector. 2.3 Research question This motivates the central question: can a query-time detector that measures the consistency between a retrieved document and its co-retrieved context detect and suppress backdoor attacks, and how does it compare with ingestion-time filtering even when the LLM is itself backdoored via fine-tuning? The experiments forced three honest revisions. First, for the stealthiest (soft-content) attack the result was the opposite: it mimics the context, so it evades RFC while the ingestion filter catches it the finding is complementarity, not RFC superiority. Second, RFC is not unconditionally effective; its operating envelope is governed by the poison fraction of the retrieved set, which I had to characterise (sweep + PCA) rather than assert. Third, the finetuning backdoor is undefendable at the retrieval layer (ASR = 1.00), which the abstract did not anticipate. Conclusion One sentence captures the study: query-time consistency detection works only while clean documents remain the majority of a retrieved set; past that point, defence must move earlier in the pipeline. RFC, a retrieval-layer query-time detector, is viable and previously unused, but only within this characterised envelope: it near-perfectly detects sparse, off-centroid corpus poison (AUC 0.99–1.00) and restores answer accuracy end-to-end, yet it cannot touch a fine-tuning backdoor and is evaded by context-mimicking poison. Because evading one layer’s signal forces producing the other’s, RFC and ingestion filtering are complementary by construction, and an adaptive attacker cannot defeat both at once. The contribution is therefore not a detector that beats the baseline, but the first precise characterisation of where retrieval-layer detection helps and where it structurally cannot defending
